title: Greg Clark: From Middlesbrough To Minister
author: Greg Clark

dom.t: Automation education: Adaptability helps but cannot suffice

st.t: Automation education: Adaptability helps but cannot suffice
st.an: Clark supports the cluster’s educational and adaptability agenda: automation increases the need for cognitive education, machine-interaction skills and preparation for changing tasks. He does not claim education is sufficient, but he also does not examine the cluster’s broader limits involving work scarcity, geography, occupational identity or technology-sector power.
qs: And so you both need to, I think, have a a more developed kind of cognitive education.
Technology moves very fast and you need to be able to do different things from from what you started doing.

kp.k: AI extends automation into knowledge-based legal work
kp.d: Host Philip Young frames AI as analogous to industrial mechanisation, but applied to knowledge-based jobs. He describes the legal profession as simultaneously excited about AI's possibilities and worried about its implications for lawyers. This is a broad framing, not a measured finding about task displacement or employment.
qs: the interesting thing for me about the AI revolution is it's sort of doing a similar thing but for very much knowledge based jobs.
my profession the legal profession has been simultaneously excited about the possibilities of AI but simultaneously worried about what it might mean for the profession and for for lawyers.

kp.k: Automation requires broader education and continuing adaptability
kp.d: Clark argues that automation has displaced mechanical activities formerly performed by school-leavers, increasing the importance of cognitive education and skills for interacting with machines. He expects workers to change activities over their careers and recommends broad early education alongside confidence to pursue interests beyond peer expectations. These are general workforce recommendations rather than a specific programme for training lawyers.
qs: You can't rely on essentially doing mechanical things. Your brain is important in virtually all jobs.
interacting with machines is something that requires skills and abilities and and training
That is vanishingly rare that someone will do precisely the same thing when they start to when they finish.
they probably also need to have instilled in them the confidence to be interested in things that perhaps their schoolmates and and friends are not.

kp.k: Active government should sustain the UK's AI ecosystem
kp.d: Clark advocates active government support for AI, invoking US public-sector technology development and government funding of education and research. He reports that most reviews place the UK perhaps third behind the US and China in AI ecosystem and company strength, without identifying those reviews. His concern is prospective: neglect could allow more ambitious countries to erode that position.
qs: First of all, I think the government should be active.
Most reviews consider us to be perhaps third in the world in terms of the strength of our AI ecosystem and companies after the US and China.
It would be an appalling thing if through neglect our position of strength was transmitted was lost to other countries that perhaps aren't as strong but uh are more ambitious.

kp.k: Support discovery research and targeted AI applications
kp.d: Clark recommends funding both open-ended discovery research and applied collaboration between research institutions and companies. He describes a UK DARPA-style body as accepting greater risk and estimates its funding, explicitly uncertainly, at about a billion pounds over a 5year period or more. Recalling his 2016 industrial strategy, he says AI and data analysis were selected as grand challenges and received applied research funding. His recommendation recognises that government cannot fund every field equally.
qs: I think the government should fund what's often called blue sky research, discovery research
I think about a billion pounds over a 5year period or something probably even more
when I developed the industrial strategy that I did in uh 2016, um we identified what we call some grand challenges
And one of them was AI and the analysis of data.
we put a lot of applied research funding in that so that institutions, universities and research bodies could work with companies to develop applications
You can't fund every single branch to the to the extent that they might merit.

kp.k: Prefer sector regulators over a central AI regulator
kp.d: Clark endorses regulating AI through existing regulators' expertise in its effects rather than treating it as wholly separate. He worries that the EU's interventionist approach could chill experimentation and deployment, and expresses a preference closer to the American model against central regulation. These are policy judgements; the transcript supplies no comparative measurement of regulatory effects. He nevertheless supports controls where AI produces socially unacceptable effects.
qs: I think at this stage in the development uh of AI we shouldn't be cutting off its progress prematurely.
I thought risk sort of chilling the the development and the the experimentation including deployment of AI in Europe
I think the UK approach which has been just as you said to to work through existing regulators I think that is the right approach
by doing it through the regulators you're looking at its effects
I'm closer to to the American model in terms of my preferences for uh for not imposing a kind of central regulation here.

kp.k: Existing legal traditions must inform AI governance
kp.d: Clark identifies intellectual property ownership and returns, copyright and privacy as questions that require established legal expertise. He argues that an AI-specialist regulator alone would not resolve intellectual property issues satisfactorily and that the Information Commissioner's Office should have powers to address AI applications. The recommendation is to adapt governance through existing legal traditions, not assume existing law needs no reconsideration.
qs: you can't simply have that and then not not be active in seeing how AI changes the the relevance of those laws.

I don't think just appointing some new AI regulator that knows about AI is going to be able to resolve that in any way satisfactory without drawing on the expertise there is in intellectual property law and copyright uh law.
the information commissioner's office is set up to be our privacy regulator they should have the powers to be able to deal with the applications of AI there

kp.k: Innovation does not override anti-discrimination protections
kp.d: Clark rejects an unrestricted technology-sector view that policymakers should simply withdraw. Using a hypothetical employment application that systematically disadvantages people of color or women, he argues that established equality protections require engagement with AI. He does not report an observed case or measured bias rate; the example explains why welcoming AI remains compatible with public-policy intervention.
qs: were you to find that a that kind of AI models or their applications were systematically disadvantaging people of color or women uh in employment markets
you can't suddenly think well that's fine with you know what can you do that's just how the AI works
Battles have been fought to provide that degree of protection and equality
I do think there's a very important space for public policy

kp.k: Garfield's founder credits sector-specific regulation with enabling entry
kp.d: Young says he deliberately built Garfield as a regulated product and attributes part of its emergence in the UK, rather than another jurisdiction, to the sector-specific regulatory approach. This is the founder's explanation, not independently established causal evidence. He emphasises accountability and responsibility, extending those requirements to foundational LLMs because he sees them as concentrating power.
qs: I took the conscious decision very early on that Garfield should be regulated and I was going to build something that would be a regulated product.
part of the reason that it's come about here as opposed to on continental Europe or somewhere else is because we did take a sector specific regulation approach to it
the two words I've used a lot in my public sort of pronouncements over the last year in the various speeches I've given are accountability and responsibility
they concentrate a lot of power into a relatively small group of hands
whenever you have power that is concentrated, you need to make sure it's accountable and it's exercised responsibly.

kp.k: Trustworthy regulation can support competition and innovation
kp.d: Clark argues that competition law and dependable legal protections can contribute positively to a contested technology market rather than merely obstruct it. Drawing an analogy with the international appeal of English law and London's financial services, he proposes that supportive regulation offering protection against malpractice could enhance the UK's technological strengths. This is a conditional competitive-advantage argument, not evidence of realised AI-market outcomes.
qs: antitrust law, competition law uh has been very important in this country and as it happens in America.
They can help the the development of a vigorous contested space.
there is both a kind of rigor to it, a dependability and that offers protections that are valuable.
for policy and regulation if we get it right this can enhance the strengths of our technological expertise rather than be in opposition to it.

kp.k: Regional innovation depends on crossing industrial boundaries
kp.d: Responding to Young's question about spreading AI innovation beyond London, Clark points to connections among gaming technology, automotive design and testing, manufacturing, and data-intensive motorsport. He argues that regional strengths can generate innovation where sectors and academic disciplines meet, and recommends enabling those connections through education and policy. These examples supply an industrial analogy rather than evidence of regional legal-services transformation.
qs: the boundaries between industrial sectors, if I can call it that, that were previously thought to be pretty rigid.
These things are breaking down.
the work that's done often with the University of Warick involved between the gamers in Lamington Spar and the designers in Jaguar Land Rover
the cluster of F1 teams there which are rely on manufacturing but they also rely on a lot of analysis and data handling.
it's often the case at the at the kind of interstitials of those sectors and indeed academic disciplines for that matter. This is where the most interesting discoveries and innovation takes place.

kp.k: Technologists and policymakers need deliberate mutual engagement
kp.d: Clark concludes that disciplinary and institutional silos persist unless actively challenged, including within universities and between government and technology developers. He urges those developing or using technology not to leave policy exclusively to politicians and civil servants. Young likewise describes innovation as requiring talent, regulators, finance and lawyers who ensure workable legal structures.
qs: this requires an effort, a deliberate effort
we need to kind of break down those barriers and I think between government and and technologists that's also uh important as well.
they absolutely need to be able to have a mutual understanding it seems to me

You don't just need the the talent to build the products. You need the regulators who will allow the right things to be built. You need the ability to finance where finance is required. you need lawyers to to ensure that the legal structure works.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Greg Clark principally makes cross-domain claims about AI regulation, innovation and workforce skills, rather than predictions about legal-service delivery or lawyer employment.
pts.d: Clark predicts that AI will become more pervasive and potentially dominant. He argues that premature, centralised AI regulation risks chilling experimentation and deployment, while existing sector regulators can address AI's effects using their substantive expertise. For legal institutions, he claims that AI raises intellectual-property, privacy and discrimination questions that require engagement with existing law and its underlying protections, rather than treatment as an entirely separate technological subject. He also claims that dependable, innovation-supportive regulation could strengthen the UK's AI competitive position by providing trust and protection against malpractice. Beyond regulation, he links automation and rapid technological change to greater needs for cognitive education, machine-interaction skills and career adaptability. He identifies collaboration across industries and academic disciplines as an opportunity for regional innovation. These are Clark's claims; the host's separate statements about knowledge-work automation and Garfield's regulatory history are not attributed to Clark.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Clark relies on policy experience, institutional examples and historical analogies; the interview supplies no quantitative evaluation of AI's effects on legal services.
pts.d: Clark invokes his experience developing the 2016 industrial strategy and funding applied AI research, alongside examples of public support for technological development through DARPA, universities and research institutions. His regulatory argument draws on the history of intellectual-property law, parliamentary protections against discrimination, antitrust enforcement and the perceived dependability of English law. His regional-innovation argument cites collaboration between gaming developers around Leamington Spa, the University of Warwick and Jaguar Land Rover, plus the data-intensive motorsport cluster. These examples support a general innovation argument rather than demonstrating measured AI outcomes. He refers to unspecified reviews ranking the UK approximately third in AI strength, and to a growing consensus about European regulation, without identifying studies. The employment-discrimination example is hypothetical, not a reported finding. There are no legal-task benchmarks, productivity measurements, client-outcome data or lawyer-displacement estimates.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Clark distinguishes immediate regulatory choices from an undated future of wider AI adoption; the anticipated benefits depend on active support, appropriate safeguards and deliberate collaboration.
pts.d: His caution against constraining AI is explicitly tied to its current developmental stage, not a claim that regulation is never appropriate. He favours sector-led intervention where AI produces unacceptable effects and insists that existing equality protections must continue to apply. The UK's prospective advantage is conditional on getting regulation right and maintaining government engagement; he warns that neglect could allow more ambitious countries to overtake it. Workforce adaptation is framed as an ongoing consequence of technological change across working lives, with particular emphasis on education while young. Cross-sector innovation requires deliberate efforts to overcome institutional silos. No date is given for AI becoming dominant, nor any timetable for changes in legal employment or service costs.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are primarily technology businesses, regulators, rights-holders, workers, young people and regional innovation communities—not specified law-firm segments.
pts.d: UK AI developers and researchers could gain from public support and trusted regulation, while European developers and adopters could face inhibited experimentation under the approach Clark criticises. Intellectual-property rights-holders face questions about ownership and returns; individuals face privacy and discrimination risks; women and people of colour are specifically identified in his hypothetical employment example. Existing regulators and policymakers must work with technologists and legal expertise. Workers need adaptable skills, and young people need broader cognitive education. Regional firms, universities, manufacturing businesses and creative industries could benefit from cross-sector collaboration. Although the podcast is introduced as concerning access to justice, Clark provides no concrete forecast of expanded legal access, reduced legal fees, changed law-firm staffing or replacement of lawyers.
